land.text: the Chengdu Plain, annexed by Qin in 316 and made a commandery (Shu jun)

successors.note: A Kaiming marquisate (Marquis Yaotong from 314, last marquis Wan put to death in 285) survived under a Qin governor; it is not drawn as a state.

capitals.name: Jinsha (Chengdu)
capitals.note: The Shu page names no capital. The Jinsha page: after Sanxingdui declined, 'Jinsha is thought to have emerged as the capital of the Shu state'; the settlement 'ended abruptly' between 500 and 200 BCE, so the dot after that is the researcher's carry-over; the page does not name the Kaiming capital.

correction.text: the Chengdu Plain in the western Sichuan basin, 'with some extension northeast to the upper Han River valley' (the Shu page gives no boundary)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria lacks Shu). The Shu page places the state on the Chengdu Plain, 'with some extension northeast to the upper Han River valley', and gives no area (infobox 'Area: not given'), so there is no figure to compare. Radius 130 km round Chengdu covers the plain only; the northeastern extension is not quantified. One shape for the whole life: the page dates no territorial change inside it.

region.text: the Chengdu Plain in the western Sichuan basin, 'with some extension northeast to the upper Han River valley' (the Shu page gives no boundary)

ledger.note: 1046 BC: Shu is on record as an ally of King Wu of Zhou at Muye. The page's infobox gives 'Established: ?'; 'Shu allied with King Wu of Zhou at the Battle of Muye' in 1046 BCE (per the Shujing) is its first dated appearance, used here as the start year. The state's real origin is undated.

666 BC: the Kaiming dynasty takes the throne. 'In 666 BCE a man from Chu called Bieling ("turtle spirit") founded the Kaiming dynasty', which lasted twelve generations until the Qin conquest: same state, same colour (rule 2).

region.text: the Chengdu Plain in the western Sichuan basin, 'with some extension northeast to the upper Han River valley' (the Shu page gives no boundary)

ledger.note: 316 BC: Qin conquers Shu. 'About 316 BCE' Qin took up Sima Cuo's proposal to annex Shu; the Kaiming king lost several battles near Jiameng and 'was captured and killed at Wuyang'; Shu became a Qin commandery. The Qin (state) page agrees: 'In 316 BC, Qin completed the conquests of the southern states of Ba and Shu, in modern Sichuan.' Region is the researcher's reading of 'Chengdu Plain'.

region.text: the Chengdu Plain in the western Sichuan basin, 'with some extension northeast to the upper Han River valley' (the Shu page gives no boundary)

ledger.note: 316 BC: the Kaiming kingdom of Shu ends in Qin conquest. The last king is killed at Wuyang; his son is made Marquis Yaotong in 314 beside a Qin governor, and the last Kaiming marquis, Wan, is put to death in 285 (not drawn as a state).

wars.name: Qin conquest of Shu and Ba

zones.text: the Chengdu Plain in the western Sichuan basin, 'with some extension northeast to the upper Han River valley' (the Shu page gives no boundary)

wars.outcome: Qin victory: Shu annexed as a commandery in 316; Ba taken the same year (see the ba dossier).
wars.note: Disagreement between pages: the Shu page has the armies meeting 'near Jiameng on the Jialing River, in Ba territory' and Qin annexing Ba afterwards; the Ba page has Ba and Chu allied with Qin against Shu before Qin turned on them. Both give 316.

wars.name: Shu-Qin clash near Hanzhong
wars.outcome: A clash only: 'in 387 Shu and Qin troops clashed near Hanzhong on the upper Han river'; the page gives no result and no change of border.
wars.note: Empty zones: the page does not say who held Hanzhong, so no contest is drawn.

certainty.note: No boundary is documented for Shu; the extent is the Chengdu Plain from the archaeology and the page's one-line 'extension northeast to the upper Han'. Soft throughout.

notes: Pages opened (4): Shu (state), Sanxingdui, Jinsha site, Qin (state). BUDGET: 2-5 pages. Wikidata id left null (Wikidata unreachable and the id is not in a page opened). START -1046 is the first dated mention (Muye alliance), not a founding: the page's infobox says 'Established: ?'. Sanxingdui (c. 1700-c. 1150 BC, walled city c. 1600 BC, 3.6 km2, Guanghan) is identified with Shu by 'many Chinese archaeologists' but the pages give a gap (1150-1046) and the identification is not certain, so it is written as its own culture dossier (sanxingdui-culture) rather than folded into the life of the state. CAPITAL: only Jinsha (thought, after Sanxingdui) is on the pages; no Kaiming capital is named; the Chengdu city wall is Qin-era. AREA: no infobox area, so no comparison with Cliopatria (which has no Shu row). NOT DRAWN: the 314-285 Kaiming marquisate under a Qin governor (Marquis Yaotong, Marquis Hui to 301, Wan to 285); the Qin side (qin dossier) carries gain from shu and ba in 316. The Stone Cattle Road, the Dujiangyan (undated on the page) and the 281 BCE Chu general who 'declared himself an independent king' beyond Shu (Dian, see that dossier if written) are not territory. Page silent on Hanzhong: the 387 clash is in wars with empty zones.
